So I say to my friend at the day job “We are bored sometimes, and scented like realtors but if everyone’s equally disconsolate under labor’s gooey caul then nuance can be stitched more vividly to secrets lodged inside of everyone until it becomes your own country with highways that carry you silently past the jetty which, from their heavy drinking, the case managers come out to failing to be stable and badly attempting to sing” We’re pushing our barques past the mansions as I say this, near the dwellings of persons whose lives have no mooring outside the slow fact of our passing— huddled arrogantly under their air-conditioning they want us to be users moved by advertisers enticing the constituency to join them and sit there and weep But we’re too busy pulling toward centers where workers assemble. While time for them is a melody played at long intervals across condominiums we who are the power know our systems so much better now come to this hour outside it now give it new form on guitar

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The speaker confronts alienating, monotonous labor and consumerist privilege by turning shared worker discontent into collective imagination, movement, and song. Workers discover their power through solidarity and systemic awareness, transforming imposed time and instability into a new social form.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: But, While

outputs.L1:
So I say to my friend at the day job, “We are bored sometimes and scented like realtors, but if everyone is equally disconsolate beneath labor’s gooey caul, then nuance can be stitched more vividly to the secrets lodged inside everyone, until it becomes your own country—with highways that carry you silently past the jetty, from which the case managers emerge after their heavy drinking, failing to be stable and badly attempting to sing.”

As I say this, we are pushing our barques past the mansions, near the dwellings of people whose lives have no mooring beyond the slow fact of our passing. Huddled arrogantly beneath their air-conditioning, they want us to be users, moved by advertisers enticing the constituency to join them, sit there, and weep. But we are too busy pulling toward the centers where workers assemble.

While time, for them, is a melody played at long intervals across condominiums, we who are the power know our systems so much better now. Come to this hour, outside it now, and give it new form on guitar.
outputs.L2:
At my regular job, I tell a friend: “At times we have nothing to do, and we smell like real-estate agents. Yet when labor’s sticky membrane leaves everybody equally dejected, subtleties can be sewn more brightly onto the private things hidden in each person, until they form a nation of your own—one threaded with highways that bear you soundlessly beyond the jetty, where case managers emerge after drinking heavily, unable to remain steady and making a poor effort at song.”

As I speak, we propel our small boats alongside the mansions, close to homes occupied by people whose existence is anchored to nothing beyond the gradual reality of our movement past them. Gathered with smugness beneath their air conditioners, they expect us to become consumers, steered by advertisers who coax the voting public to come sit beside them and cry.

But our hands are occupied with rowing toward the places where laborers gather. For those people, time resembles a tune sounded only occasionally across the condominiums. We, however—the source of power—understand our systems far more clearly now. Arrive at this moment, step beyond it, and reshape it with a guitar.
outputs.L3:
The speaker and a coworker feel bored and disheartened by the alienating conditions of their labor. Their work seems monotonous and disconnected from any meaningful sense of purpose, leaving them emotionally detached from both what they produce and the world around them. Yet their shared dissatisfaction also creates an opening for honesty. By recognizing the same frustration in one another, they uncover personal truths that might otherwise remain hidden and begin to imagine a different kind of belonging—one grounded in mutual understanding rather than in work, status, or consumption.

In contrast, the wealthy residents remain isolated within the comfort of their private lives. Their way of living depends on distance from others and on the expectation that ordinary people will accept the roles assigned to them. Advertising reinforces this arrangement by encouraging individuals to become passive consumers, defining themselves through the products they buy instead of through their relationships, labor, or creative capacities.

The speaker and their companions reject this passivity. Rather than remaining trapped in isolation or submitting to consumer culture, they move toward public spaces where workers gather and act collectively. In these shared environments, workers recognize that they are not powerless individuals but members of a larger community with the ability to challenge existing conditions. Through solidarity and creativity, they seek to reshape not only systems of labor and social organization but also their experience of time itself. Their collective action points toward a society in which people can reclaim control over their lives and build more meaningful forms of work, community, and freedom.
outputs.L4:
The speaker begins from the alienating reality of monotonous labor: repetitive tasks, regulated hours, and a workplace that reduces human beings to units of productivity. This exhaustion exists alongside a consumer culture whose comforts and privileges conceal the labor that sustains them. Yet the workers’ shared dissatisfaction does not remain private or passive. As they recognize their common condition, frustration becomes imagination, and imagination becomes collective action. Their bodies begin to move together, while their separate voices gather into song, creating a communal language capable of challenging the order imposed upon them.

Through solidarity, the workers discover that their apparent weakness and instability are not individual failures but products of a larger system. This awareness allows them to see themselves not merely as isolated employees but as a social force with the power to reshape their circumstances. Time once controlled by schedules, wages, and repetitive production is reclaimed as a space for connection and possibility. By acting, moving, and singing together, the workers transform alienation into community and precarity into shared strength. Their collective energy points toward a new social form—one organized not around consumption, hierarchy, and imposed labor, but around mutual recognition, creative freedom, and common purpose.
outputs.L5:
### A Busy Weekend

I wanted to relax this weekend, **but** I had many things to do. **While** I was cleaning the house, my sister prepared lunch. We were both tired, **but** we continued working. **While** we ate, we talked about our plans for the evening. I wanted to watch a movie, **but** my sister preferred to go for a walk. In the end, we did both and had a wonderful day.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about alienated workers traveling by boat past wealthy mansions and condominiums toward a place of collective labor and solidarity.
counterfactuals.output:
At dawn the workers boarded a boat made of punched clocks and blue tin. No one spoke. Their names slept in their pockets beside bolts, bus transfers, and bread wrapped in yesterday’s weather.

The river carried them past mansions with marble eyelids. Behind the glass, chandeliers grazed like captive constellations, and pale dogs dreamed on rugs thick as silence. Condominiums rose from the banks, immaculate and unblinking, each balcony holding a small, decorative loneliness. Above the penthouses, private clouds waited for permission to rain.

The workers watched their reflections break beneath the oars. For years they had tightened the screws in other people’s mornings, lifted boxes full of invisible profit, polished floors until their own faces disappeared. Now the foreman’s whistle was far behind them, circling the abandoned factory like a mechanical bird.

The boat moved on. It passed a fountain pouring coins instead of water. It passed a garden where every flower wore a lock. It passed a dining room in which twelve empty chairs consumed a golden animal.

Then the river widened.

Ahead, smoke rose—not the black handwriting of the old furnaces, but the warm breath of communal kitchens. On the shore stood carpenters, nurses, cleaners, teachers, welders, and those whose jobs had never been given names. They were raising a roof broad enough to shelter disagreement. They were repairing the nets, sharing the hammers, teaching the machines a different grammar.

Someone on the boat began to sing. The song had no owner. One by one, the others entered it, carrying their cracked voices like useful tools.

When they reached the landing, the boat unfolded into a long table.

They stepped ashore together, and behind them the mansions dwindled into porcelain teeth. Before them, the day waited in work clothes, many-handed and unfinished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental, stream-of-consciousness political poem that blends office boredom, class struggle, advertising, alcoholism, waterfront imagery, and music.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE REVOLUTION WILL BE PUT ON HOLD**

At 3:17 the spreadsheet begins to breathe—  
green cells, little rented lawns,  
numbers grazing under fluorescent weather  
while Janice reheats fish  
and somewhere a printer coughs up  
the minutes of the previous defeat.

I am paid by the hour to forget the hour.

Outside, the harbor shoulders its iron coat.  
Cranes bow and rise, bow and rise,  
red priests blessing the containers—  
sneakers, televisions, plastic saints,  
all shipped in under the slogan

**YOU DESERVE MORE**

in a font the color of clean teeth.

More what?  
More Tuesday? More passwords?  
More executive laughter leaking  
through the conference-room glass?

The boss says *we’re a family*  
and the family says *union*  
and the boss says *not like that.*

Down by Pier Nine, gulls tear open  
a black bag of market research.  
The tide thumbs oil across the pilings.  
A freighter groans in B minor,  
slow blues for the globally outsourced,  
and a dockworker taps the rhythm  
with a wrench against the rail—

clang, clang,  
who owns the morning?  
clang, clang,  
who drank the wage?

At lunch I buy a bottle  
the color of resignation,  
pour one small promotion into coffee,  
then another, then another.  
By five, my liver is a picket line  
with nobody crossing.

The radio plays brass—  
wild, democratic trumpets  
climbing the cubicle walls,  
a bass walking out without permission,  
drums distributing thunder equally  
among all departments.

I type:

Dear Sir or Madam,  
please find attached  
the sea.

Please find attached  
eight million exhausted hands.

Please find attached  
the moon over the warehouse district,  
stamped **CLEARANCE**,  
slashed from heaven’s original price.

An advertisement floats above the expressway:

**LIVE YOUR BEST LIFE**

and beneath it a man sleeps in his car  
with the engine off to save gasoline.  
The billboard woman smiles  
as if hunger were a whitening treatment.

Night clocks in.

The waterfront neon trembles  
inside every broken bottle.  
Ships drag their chains through black water.  
From the tavern comes an old song—  
piano missing three teeth,  
voice rough as rope:

*We built the city, baby,*  
*but the city billed us rent.*

Everyone joins on the chorus,  
even the office towers,  
their thousand lit windows  
like eyes refusing to close,  
even the photocopier dreaming  
of multiplying bread,  
even Janice, even the gulls,  
even me with my tie loosened  
into a small red flag—

and for one impossible measure  
the harbor stops importing silence.

The cranes hold their breath.

The glasses rise.

The workers rise.

The music, drunk and shining,  
refuses to come down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense prose-poetry passage in which the speaker talks to a friend from their day job while rowing past affluent homes, contrasting isolated elites with organized workers.
counterfactuals.output: Mara, you who clock in beside me beneath the warehouse fluorescents, pull once, then feather the oar: see how the mansions lift their pale brows above the river, each window holding one immaculate loneliness, each lawn shaved smooth as silence, each dock chained to its private absence. Their lamps come on singly; their wealth is a row of locked rooms pretending to be a city. But we know another architecture—the break-room table crowded with thermoses, the loading bay where names pass mouth to mouth, the union hall bright with wet coats and raised hands. We know how a grievance becomes a chorus, how a chorus becomes a vote, how a vote enters the factory at dawn with ten thousand boots inside it. Let them keep their stone lions, their cameras, their hedges trained not to touch; we have learned from pallets, from rivets, from this narrow boat: nothing heavy moves unless many hands agree upon the direction. Row, friend. Behind those balconies, one heart bargains with its echo; here, shoulder to shoulder, we make the dark water answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a contemporary leftist poem with deliberately strange metaphors and long, winding sentences. Include realtors, case managers, barques, air-conditioning, advertisers, condominiums, and a guitar.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon the realtors arrive in shoes polished bright as obedient satellites,  
unlocking the condominiums where each empty room has been taught  
to pronounce *investment* without moving its mouth,  
while below, the case managers carry folders thick as winter loaves  
and try to ration mercy among families whose names  
have become red numbers blinking in the landlord’s aquarium.

The air-conditioning hums its little anthem of private weather,  
cooling the marble lobbies where advertisers, pale captains  
of invisible barques, sail across our hunger with sails stitched  
from targeted desire, whispering that freedom is a stainless-steel refrigerator,  
a wristwatch, a door no neighbor can knock upon,  
a cloud that accepts all major credit cards.

But in the courtyard someone brings a guitar, scarred and democratic,  
and strikes one chord that rolls through the towers  
like a red wheelbarrow full of thunder, like soup learning to organize,  
like every elevator suddenly refusing the penthouse  
until the basement has windows, until the janitor owns Tuesday,  
until no child must trade sleep for the arithmetic of rent.

Then the realtors lower their silver keys, the case managers  
step out from behind the barricades of paperwork,  
and even the barques turn shoreward, crowded with impossible cargo—  
free clinics, forgiven debts, peaches without patents,  
air-conditioning for the old woman on the sixth floor  
whose summer has been boiling her bones into a landlord’s tea—

and we sing, not beautifully but together, our voices long and winding  
as a union meeting held inside a comet, declaring that the city  
is not a necklace for capital to lock around the river,  
that the condominiums must open like strange metal flowers,  
that the advertisers may keep their moon made of coupons,  
because here comes the future carrying groceries in both arms,  
and it has learned, at last, to kick the door open.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an avant-garde monologue about labor alienation transforming into worker power, using nautical imagery and an ending that calls for giving time or history “new form on guitar.”
counterfactuals.output:
I clock in beneath a moon stamped PROPERTY OF THE COMPANY.

The factory is a ship that has forgotten the sea. Its windows are blind portholes; its belts keep moving because no horizon can persuade them otherwise. All night I bolt small thunder to smaller thunder. My hands depart from me piece by piece, packed into crates with numbers instead of names.

At dawn, the foreman says, *Good work.*

But whose work?

The question swims through the fluorescent water. It brushes every ankle. It grows gills in the break room.

We sit around a table nailed to the bottom of the hour. Rosa unwraps her lunch. Malik rubs the red harbor of his wrist. Someone laughs—not because anything is funny, but because laughter is a smuggler. It carries us across borders the clock cannot patrol.

I used to think I was alone in the engine room, shoveling my breath into a furnace owned by strangers. I used to think exhaustion was private weather.

Then the walls began answering.

Not with words at first: with coughs, with boots, with chairs scraping backward at the same moment. A rough tide of recognition. My fatigue was yours. Your missing finger was ours. The wage that divided us became the rope that showed how tightly we had all been tied.

So we learned the grammar of knots.

We tied refusal to memory.  
We tied memory to demand.  
We tied demand to every hand the ship had called replaceable.

And suddenly the vessel trembled—not from the captain’s command, but from the knowledge of the rowers.

We stopped.

What an enormous sound a stopped machine makes.

In that silence, the factory remembered it was built by bodies. The conveyor became only metal. The schedule became only ink. The foreman’s voice, stripped of our obedience, fluttered like a flag over an abandoned mast.

We looked at one another and saw not cogs, not cargo, not rented muscles, but a crew.

No—more than a crew.

The sea itself, standing up.

Now we steer by a constellation assembled from our scars. We chart a course where bread is not ransom, where hours do not disappear into another man’s vault, where the hands that raise the sail decide the destination.

The old world calls this mutiny.

Let it.

Every just shore was once accused of moving.

Bring the drum. Bring the salt. Bring the names of those thrown overboard and those who taught the drowned to sing. We have been kept below deck long enough.

Tonight we take back the compass.

Tomorrow we give history new form on guitar.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
